idiom_name: structuredClone(state) pushed onto a history array
implementation_notes: JavaScript states are object graphs, so the modern memento is a deep copy: structuredClone runs the structured clone algorithm synchronously and returns a fully detached value, preserving cycles and handling Date, Map, Set, RegExp and ArrayBuffer - a direct replacement for the JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) that predates it. The originator owns the state object, the caretaker is an array or capped stack that pushes clones and pops them on undo, and #private fields keep the originator's own state out of reach. Because the clone is plain data (functions and DOM nodes are not clonable, and the prototype chain is not walked), restoring means feeding the snapshot back through the originator rather than reviving it as a live object.
pitfalls: structuredClone only handles structured-cloneable data: functions and DOM nodes throw DataCloneError, the prototype chain is not walked and class private elements are not duplicated, so a snapshot is plain data that the originator must rehydrate.
Property descriptors, getters and setters are not preserved - a derived property computed by a getter becomes a fixed value in the snapshot, which then goes stale if it is read as if it were live.
The JSON round-trip fallback is lossy: undefined, functions, symbols and Date types degrade (to null/strings), so it silently captures less state than the code believes.
An unbounded history array keeps whole state graphs alive; cap the depth or drop the oldest entry on push.

variants.name: Frozen immutable state with spread updates
variants.idiom_name: Object.freeze + spread-created successor states, previous values as mementos
variants.implementation_notes: The functional realization never mutates state: every change replaces it with a new object built by spreading the previous one, so a snapshot is simply the previous value the caretaker still references - no copying at all, because sharing immutable values is safe. Object.freeze is the highest integrity level JavaScript offers and turns accidental writes into failures, but it is shallow, so nested structures must be frozen recursively (or treated as immutable by discipline). This is the model behind Redux-style state containers and React state updates: history is a stack of previous states and undo re-selects one.
pitfalls: Object.freeze is shallow: freezing the top-level object leaves nested arrays and objects mutable, so history can still be corrupted through a nested reference.
Writes to a frozen object fail silently in sloppy mode and throw only in strict mode or modules - a test that never enables strict mode can miss the bug.
Objects with elements cannot be frozen (freeze on a non-empty TypedArray or DataView throws), so binary buffers must be copied instead of frozen.
Spreading allocates a new top-level object per update but shares nested values; an in-place edit of a nested value mutates every snapshot that references it.
